forces.title: Consumers increasingly prioritize health, avoiding fast food due to GLP-1 impact
forces.description: The growing adoption of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and an increasing focus on healthy aging among consumers are fundamentally reshaping demand for food and drink. Consumers, especially 'longevity seekers,' are actively avoiding fast food, leading to reduced portion sizes, healthier menu choices, and decreased frequency of QSR visits. This necessitates a strategic repositioning for restaurants, moving beyond traditional offerings to align with evolving health-conscious consumption patterns.
forces.source_title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?

forces.title: Rise of solo households creates new demand for tailored restaurant offerings
forces.description: The global increase in solo households, projected to exceed 45% in some OECD countries by 2050, represents a significant demographic shift. This trend creates new demand patterns for services supporting independent living, including restaurants. Operators have an opportunity to innovate by redesigning products, formats, and dining experiences to cater specifically to the needs and preferences of one-person households, potentially unlocking substantial growth in this underserved segment.
forces.source_title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?

forces.title: AI-enabled purchasing agents reshape consumer discovery and transactions
forces.description: The rapid evolution of AI models and the emergence of autonomous purchasing agents are fundamentally altering how consumers discover and buy products and services, including food. AI systems are becoming critical 'gatekeepers of brand visibility,' interpreting consumer intent and curating shortlists before direct engagement with retailers. Restaurants must adapt by focusing on 'generative engine optimization' (GEO) and ensuring their offerings are accessible, interpretable, and trusted by AI to remain relevant in this new tech-driven path to purchase.
forces.source_title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?

forces.title: AI-led discovery and agentic search changing how consumers find products
forces.description: The shift to AI-led discovery is accelerating, with 70% of UK consumers using conversational AI platforms and 38% for shopping tasks. AI systems now interpret intent and curate product shortlists, compressing the path to purchase and reducing the influence of traditional search and brand websites. Restaurants need a joined-up visibility strategy with structured product data and first-party insights to remain visible and competitive in journeys increasingly shaped by AI before a customer even reaches a website.
forces.source_title: Retail resilience

forces.title: GLP-1 drug adoption drives significant reduction in restaurant spending
forces.description: The increasing use of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs is causing a significant reduction in consumer spending on food away from home. Active users are ordering fewer items, skipping sides, seeking healthier restaurants, customizing for health, and visiting QSRs less often. This behavioral shift, with an initial 5-20% spending decline across various dining categories, represents a substantial and likely persistent headwind for restaurant operators, impacting overall traffic and basket size.
forces.source_title: The Unexpected Ways GLP-1s Are Transforming Consumer Behavior

forces.title: GLP-1 influence shifts household consumption towards healthier eating
forces.description: GLP-1 drug usage is driving broader changes in household consumption habits beyond individual users. Survey data shows significant shifts towards healthier food choices, increased fruit and vegetable consumption, reduced fast food/takeout, higher protein intake, and smaller portion sizes at mealtimes. This structural shift in consumer preferences, affecting entire households, compels restaurants to re-evaluate their menu offerings and marketing strategies to cater to a more health-conscious customer base.
forces.source_title: The Unexpected Ways GLP-1s Are Transforming Consumer Behavior

forces.title: Warm summer weather drives increased consumer spending in eating and drinking
forces.description: Consistent warm weather during the summer months in the UK is acting as a significant tailwind for the Eating and Drinking sector. Increased consumer confidence and desire for social occasions and days out contribute to a boost in spending at pubs, bars, cafes, and restaurants. This cyclical factor supports overall Hospitality & Leisure spend, demonstrating how favorable weather conditions can drive short-term demand and positive growth for food service operators.
forces.source_title: UK Consumer Spend

forces.title: Consumer concerns over prices, shrinkflation, and skimpflation impact spending
forces.description: Despite improving consumer confidence, a vast majority (84%) remain concerned about rising prices, and over three-quarters cite 'shrinkflation' (77%) and 'skimpflation' (76%) as worries. This heightened cost and quality consciousness means consumers are actively seeking better deals and scrutinizing value. For restaurants, this poses a key risk as they must carefully manage pricing, portion sizes, and perceived food quality to avoid alienating budget-sensitive customers and losing sales to more affordable alternatives.
forces.source_title: UK Consumer Spend

forces.title: UK household spending sees modest growth, boosting consumer services
forces.description: UK household spending is projected to grow around +1.0% in 2026, supported by public sector wage hikes. While this provides a welcome near-term boost, it's not yet a structural recovery. For consumer services, including restaurants, this represents a cautious tailwind, offering some uplift in demand. However, the modest growth rate and ongoing sticky inflation mean businesses still need to budget for constrained consumer finances and manage costs effectively.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Persistent high inflation and rising borrowing costs constrain consumer spending
forces.description: The UK economy faces sticky inflation (forecast at +2.9% in 2026) and elevated borrowing costs, with the Bank Rate expected to reach 4.00%. This environment significantly increases financing costs for businesses and erodes household disposable income, making consumers more cautious about discretionary spending. For restaurants, this translates into reduced demand, pressure on profitability due to higher operational costs, and elevated credit risk across the supply chain, necessitating proactive financial management.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Elevated corporate insolvencies necessitate proactive credit risk management
forces.description: Corporate insolvencies remain elevated across Western Europe, with a forecast increase of +2% in 2026. This macro-level risk extends to the restaurant sector, where financial stress can quickly disrupt supply chains and customer relationships. Businesses need to adopt a proactive approach to managing customer credit risk, closely assessing the financial strength of counterparties to safeguard cash flow and ensure operational continuity in an uncertain economic climate.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Rising consumer prices and trade-down behaviors dampen discretionary spending
forces.description: Global consumers are grappling with rising prices, geopolitical instability, and energy price volatility, leading over three-quarters to engage in trade-down behaviors. This includes optimizing essential purchases (switching brands, smaller pack sizes) and re-evaluating discretionary spending. For restaurants, this signifies a significant headwind as consumers become more resourceful, prioritize value, and are willing to 'DIY' services or extend product lifespans, shifting away from dining out unless perceived value is exceptionally high.
forces.source_title: State of the Consumer 2026: When tech acceleration and cost pressures collide

forces.title: Grocery discount retailers intensify value competition for restaurants
forces.description: The aggressive growth of grocery discount retailers like Aldi and Lidl in the UK is forcing incumbents to rethink pricing, product quality, and cost structures. This trend, playing out across various consumer categories, poses a significant key risk to restaurants. As grocery stores offer increasingly competitive value propositions for food consumed at home, restaurants face heightened pressure to justify their prices and differentiate their offerings, potentially impacting their market share and profitability if they cannot compete on perceived value.
forces.source_title: State of the Consumer 2026: When tech acceleration and cost pressures collide

forces.title: Restaurant price inflation outpaces grocery, driving consumers to eat at home
forces.description: Restaurant price inflation has significantly exceeded grocery price increases (13.6% vs 5.5% in the US between Jan 2023-Mar 2026), making food away from home comparatively more expensive. This disconnect is causing consumers, particularly those with lower and middle incomes, to shift their spending habits towards cooking at home or relying on prepared meals from grocery stores. This represents a major headwind for restaurant operators, leading to decreased traffic and sales volumes across the industry.
forces.source_title: Resetting the Restaurant Value Equation

forces.title: Widespread consumer belt-tightening reduces restaurant and food delivery spending
forces.description: A pervasive mood of belt-tightening across US and European consumers is severely impacting restaurant and food delivery operators. Survey data indicates that 41% of US consumers plan to cut back on restaurant and café spending, with 40% planning to reduce delivery/takeout. This widespread economic pressure, leading to 'the belt-tightening mood being so severe,' signals a significant headwind, requiring restaurants to adapt to a more value-conscious consumer base, even at the risk of margin erosion.
forces.source_title: Resetting the Restaurant Value Equation

forces.title: Restaurant operators wary of value plays due to potential margin erosion
forces.description: In a challenging economic environment characterized by rising costs and intense competition from grocery stores, restaurant executive teams are hesitant to implement aggressive value plays. While consumers demand affordability, brands fear that 'the wrong bold move could set a business back further than standing still' by wrecking already squeezed margins. This wariness creates a key risk, as inaction can lead to continued traffic declines, but ill-conceived promotions can severely damage profitability.
forces.source_title: Resetting the Restaurant Value Equation

forces.title: QSR market growth is inflation-driven, with real volumes flat and declining spending
forces.description: The QSR market's growth over the past three years has primarily been fueled by inflation, with underlying real volume remaining stagnant. Consumers are increasingly cutting back on QSR spending (net 6 percentage points more reducing vs. increasing), citing higher prices as the main reason. This signifies a significant headwind where operators must compete fiercely for existing market share, rather than benefiting from overall category expansion, requiring strategic adaptation to shifting consumer value perceptions.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Gen Z consumer behavior shifts towards dish splitting, deal-seeking, and 3P platforms
forces.description: Gen Z exhibits distinct QSR consumption patterns, including splitting dishes (at twice the rate of other cohorts), actively seeking promotions (around 45%), and strongly preferring third-party (3P) platforms for delivery and takeaway (50%). These behaviors indicate a structural shift in how younger consumers engage with QSR, requiring operators to adapt their menu design, promotional strategies, and 3P platform engagement to effectively capture and retain this crucial demographic.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Shift towards 3P platforms for QSR delivery necessitates distinct strategy
forces.description: With over 55% of QSR orders now digital and 50% of Gen Z preferring third-party (3P) delivery platforms, operators face a critical structural shift. Brands must develop a distinct 3P strategy, viewing platforms as customer acquisition channels rather than destinations, with tailored menus, pricing, and promotions. Failure to protect unit economics and negotiate leverage with aggregators on commissions and service levels risks subsidizing platform growth at the expense of own-channel margins and customer relationships.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Personalized loyalty programs and new occasion development drive QSR frequency
forces.description: Loyalty program members visit QSRs 1.9 times more often, highlighting the potential for personalized engagement. Designing programs to convert occasional buyers into regulars, rather than just discounting existing ones, can significantly boost frequency and basket size. Furthermore, developing offerings for underpenetrated occasions like snacking, late night, and breakfast creates new reasons for visits. These strategies, combined with tailored CRM, represent powerful levers for incremental growth and customer lifetime value.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Scaling AI for commercial and operational impact in QSR, including GEO
forces.description: AI is rapidly becoming a critical tool for QSR, with 47% of Australian consumers already using it for tasks like price comparison and restaurant research. As transactional AI grows, operators have an upside driver to scale AI for commercial and operational impact. This includes defining channel strategy, mastering Answer Engine Optimization (GEO) to ensure brand visibility in AI responses, and achieving transactional readiness with structured data. Proactive adoption can create a significant competitive advantage in customer discovery and order fulfillment.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Undifferentiated QSR brands lacking clear positioning risk losing market share
forces.description: BCG analysis shows that most major QSR players are not strongly associated with any single emotional or functional territory in consumers' minds, indicating a problem of positioning clarity. Brands that lack a sharp proposition and consistent operational execution (e.g., on service, speed, food quality) are losing significant market share. In a competitive, inflation-driven market, the risk is high for undifferentiated brands as consumers increasingly seek clear value and consistent delivery aligned with specific demand spaces.
forces.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

forces.title: Widespread financial distress among European consumers impacts discretionary spending
forces.description: Over half of European consumers (53%) are worried about their daily personal finances, an increase from 40% in 2024, indicating widespread financial distress and pessimism. This leads consumers to prioritize saving more, even with hypothetical extra income, rather than immediate discretionary spending. For restaurants, this represents a significant headwind as consumers become more cautious with their budgets, reserving dining out as a lower priority compared to building financial buffers, delaying potential recovery in demand.
forces.source_title: European Consumers Are Still Cutting Back

forces.title: Major live events drive substantial consumer spending in hospitality and leisure
forces.description: Major sporting, musical, and cultural events generate significant short-term demand spikes, with average attendee spending potentially reaching £981 for large concerts like Harry Styles' Wembley dates, contributing to over £1 billion in total consumer spending. This demand extends to hospitality, including pre- and post-event food and drink. For restaurants near event locations, this represents a strong cyclical tailwind, creating opportunities for increased sales if businesses plan for staffing, stock, and relevant propositions.
forces.source_title: Spending in Styles

forces.title: Strong consumer preference for experiences offers opportunity for value-driven restaurants
forces.description: Almost half of UK consumers (47%) prefer spending on experiences over material goods, even willing to travel or pay more for 'once-in-a-lifetime' events. This underlying consumer mindset creates an upside driver for the restaurant sector. By crafting timely, relevant, and value-driven propositions that enhance social moments or feel unique, restaurants can capitalize on this demand for experiences, attracting budget-conscious consumers who are selective about their discretionary spending but willing to pay for perceived worth.
forces.source_title: Spending in Styles

viewpoints.title: Healthy aging trend poses challenge for fast food operators
viewpoints.description: BCG's research highlights a growing cohort of 'longevity seekers' who prioritize healthy aging. This group actively avoids unhealthy habits like fast food, binge eating, and alcohol. This trend, particularly among affluent Gen X and Baby Boomers, presents a significant challenge for fast food and QSR operators who must adapt offerings to align with evolving health and wellness priorities, otherwise facing a structural decline in demand from this segment.
viewpoints.source_title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?

viewpoints.title: Rise of solo households opens new opportunities for restaurants
viewpoints.description: The proliferation of solo households, projected to reach over 45% in some OECD countries by 2050, creates a significant opportunity for the restaurant sector. Brands serving everyday independent living, including food and beverage, restaurants, and hospitality, can redesign products, formats, and experiences specifically to cater to the needs and preferences of one-person households, unlocking substantial future growth potential.
viewpoints.source_title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?

viewpoints.title: GLP-1 usage significantly reduces restaurant spending, with partial rebound
viewpoints.description: BCG research indicates that active GLP-1 users drastically reduce their spending at restaurants, with initial declines ranging from 5-20% across various dining categories (cafes, fast casual, casual dining, fine dining, quick service). While lapsed users do resume eating out, their spending remains lower than pre-GLP-1 levels. This trend poses a significant, sustained headwind for restaurant operators.
viewpoints.source_title: The Unexpected Ways GLP-1s Are Transforming Consumer Behavior

viewpoints.title: UK Eating and Drinking sector maintains summer growth amid warm weather
viewpoints.description: Barclays reports that 'Eating and Drinking' establishments, including pubs, bars, clubs, restaurants, cafes, and bakeries, sustained positive growth in August 2026. This performance, though slightly slower than July, was supported by consistently warm weather that encouraged social outings and staycations. The Head of Hospitality and Leisure noted the benefit social venues received, contributing to overall Hospitality & Leisure spend increases.

viewpoints.title: Global restaurant growth slows significantly amidst experience economy boom
viewpoints.description: McKinsey analysis reveals that global restaurant growth has decelerated to 1.2% between 2023 and 2025, less than half its pre-pandemic rate of 2.2%. This slowdown occurs despite a broader 'experience economy' where consumers prioritize meaningful moments. While luxury travel thrives, consumers remain cost-conscious, choosing lower-cost at-home alternatives, signaling a challenging environment for restaurants to attract discretionary spending.
viewpoints.source_title: State of the Consumer 2026: When tech acceleration and cost pressures collide

viewpoints.title: Restaurants losing market share to grocery stores due to price inflation
viewpoints.description: Bain identifies that restaurants are losing significant business to grocery stores because the cost of food bought away from home has risen much faster (13.6% in US between Jan 2023-Mar 2026) than food eaten at home (5.5%). This disconnect, particularly impacting low- and middle-income consumers, forces many to cook at home, leading to declines in restaurant traffic. The report emphasizes the need for restaurants to reset their value equation.

viewpoints.title: Consumer belt-tightening severely impacts restaurant and food delivery spending
viewpoints.description: Bain's survey shows a severe 'belt-tightening mood' among US and European consumers, with 41% of US consumers planning to reduce spending on restaurants and cafés, and 40% on delivery and takeout. This indicates a profound economic impact overpowering previous convenience-driven spending trends. The industry faces tough choices as executive teams grapple with adapting to financial constraints without sacrificing margins, with hesitation to implement value plays.

viewpoints.title: QSR market growth is inflation-driven, with real volumes flat and declining spending
viewpoints.description: BCG's survey of Australian QSR consumers reveals that market growth over the past three years has been primarily due to inflation, with real volumes remaining flat. Consumer spending intentions show a net reduction, with 70% of those cutting back citing higher prices. This indicates a highly competitive market where any growth must come from taking share, rather than overall category expansion, driven by cautious consumers.
viewpoints.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

viewpoints.title: Value perception in QSR encompasses service, speed, and quality beyond just price
viewpoints.description: BCG analysis of major Australian QSRs indicates that price accounts for only 36% of value perception, significantly less than in the US. Service and speed (26%), along with food quality (19%), are critical differentiators, often areas where larger players under-index. This suggests that a purely price-led strategy is insufficient, and brands must sharpen their positioning and operational execution across multiple value drivers to win consumer preference.
viewpoints.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

viewpoints.title: Proactive adaptation to structural shifts is key for QSR success
viewpoints.description: BCG asserts that winning in the evolving QSR cycle requires brands to clearly own a 'demand space', relentlessly execute on fundamentals, and proactively address structural shifts. This includes responding to increasing GLP-1 usage, leveraging AI for discovery and transactions, and strategically managing third-party delivery platforms. Brands that position themselves early, while competitors debate these trends, will gain a structural advantage in a competitive market.
viewpoints.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow

viewpoints.title: Major events expected to boost summer trading for hospitality and leisure
viewpoints.description: Barclays reports that 60% of UK hospitality and leisure leaders anticipate a positive impact on trading conditions from the summer calendar of sporting and cultural events. Major live events, like the Harry Styles concert, generate significant consumer spending including for pre- and post-event food and drink. This indicates optimism for short-term demand spikes, provided businesses prepare with relevant, value-driven propositions and strong operational planning.

demand_drivers.description: Active GLP-1 users show significant reductions in spending: Cafes (5%-10%), Fast Casual (15%-20%), Casual Dining (10%-15%), Fine Dining (5%-10%), Quick Service (20%).

market_sizing.methodology: BCG Global survey data from April 2026 (N=1882) on active GLP-1 users' self-reported changes in purchasing behavior across various dining categories.
market_sizing.source_title: The Unexpected Ways GLP-1s Are Transforming Consumer Behavior

demand_drivers.description: Overall card spending increased 2.1% in August, with non-essential spending at a 12-month high (2.1%). Strong performance in Hospitality & Leisure (+3.3%) boosted by warm weather and consumer outings.
Consistent warm weather during summer encouraged consumers to engage in social occasions and days out, benefiting bars, pubs, cafes, and restaurants.

market_sizing.methodology: UK consumer card spending data for August 2026, specifically for the 'Restaurants, Cafes and Bakeries' category.

demand_drivers.description: Australian QSR market grew 5% per year over the past three years, but this growth is primarily inflation-driven, with real volume growth being roughly flat.
More than 55% of QSR orders are now placed digitally, with Gen Z (63%) and Millennials (52%) showing high penetration.
47% of Australian consumers have used AI for at least one QSR task, with Gen Z reaching 67% (mainly for price comparison, restaurant research, nutrition checks).

market_sizing.methodology: BCG survey of 2,000 Australian QSR consumers in May 2026 and analysis of market share trends over a three-year horizon. Data on QSR digital ordering and AI usage based on specific survey questions.
market_sizing.source_title: Eat or Be Eaten: How Australian Restaurants Can Win When Volumes Slow
